column3: Exact parallel: the same claim about the Most Merciful taking a son is answered by declaring the alleged offspring honored servants.
Condemns knowingly attributing falsehood to God, the central error in the focus claim.
A false doctrinal assertion, but it concerns resurrection rather than divine sonship.
Directly warns those who say that God has taken a son.
Jesus' declaration of his birth, death, and resurrection supports his created human status within the surrounding sonship dispute.
Direct continuation stating that it is not fitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.
Explicitly exalts the Lord above taking either a spouse or a child.
Denounces those who fabricate lies about God, directly characterizing the focus claim.
Immediate continuation: it specifies that the offense is attributing a son to the Most Merciful.
Repeats the claim and refutes it through God's ownership of heaven and earth and all creatures' submission.
Identifies Jesus as son of Mary and the true word concerning the matter people dispute.
Human kinship and children have no saving power, a distant contrast to privileging filial ties.
The divine name al-Rahman is the focus claim's subject, though this verse supplies no sonship argument.
Repeats the assertion and rejects it through God's self-sufficiency, ownership, and the claimants' lack of knowledge.
Names God as the all-knowing, unique al-Rahman, providing only broad theological context.
In the same passage, it challenges an unsupported claim by asking whether its speaker has unseen knowledge or a covenant with al-Rahman.
A nearby unsupported claim to wealth and children illustrates the passage's exposure of presumptuous speech.
Uses the name al-Rahman but does not address the false attribution.
The response to the Day of Judgment does not clarify divine sonship.
Moses' admission of an earlier error has no material relation to the focus claim.
Directly denies that God should take a son and grounds creation in the command "Be."
Rejects an uninformed claim about the Most Merciful's will, paralleling the focus's unauthorized attribution.
God's recording and punishment of the speaker's words belongs to the local sequence of false claims preceding the focus.
Contrasts the firm word that God establishes with the focus's false assertion.
Immediately precedes the focus by limiting intercession to one holding a covenant with al-Rahman, not a filial privilege.
The crowd around God's servant in prayer does not illuminate the attribution of a son.
A general exposure of deniers confronted with what they rejected, without a sonship connection.
Mislabeling a sign as magic is a loose parallel to false religious speech.
The gifts given to the Children of Israel do not address the focus claim.
A false label for the messenger loosely parallels fabrication, but not divine sonship.
Directly tests and then rejects the proposition that the Most Merciful has a son.
The warning of consequences for mockery is unrelated to the false filial attribution.
Mercy as a social virtue does not clarify the title al-Rahman or divine sonship.
The plot to burn Abraham has no relevant relation to the focus.
Jesus' goodness to his mother reinforces the surrounding presentation of him as Mary’s human son.
Describes revelation from al-Rahman, offering only general context for the divine name.
The magicians' profession of faith does not bear on the claim of divine sonship.
Changing God's words is a distant parallel to unauthorized religious speech.
The disbelievers' astonishment at a warner is a generic rejection response.
Directly rejects the projection of human gendered offspring preferences onto God.
Addresses disbelievers generally but does not develop the particular false claim.
Challenges the charge that revelation was fabricated, relevant to the broader issue of fabricated religious assertions.
Explicitly denies that God has taken a son and links the denial to the incoherence of multiple gods.
The accounting of communities by their records does not clarify the focus claim.
Condemns saying what one does not do, only a broad speech-ethics parallel.
Uses the name al-Rahman without addressing the attribution of a son.
Moses' fear of being denied does not illuminate the focus.
The hypocrites' reaction to success or calamity is unrelated.
Condemns taking desire as a god, a related form of false assignment of divine authority.
Pharaoh's reminder of Moses' upbringing has no material relation.
Believers' brotherhood and mercy do not address the claim.
Taking a path back to one's Lord shares the verb only and supplies no sonship connection.
Conflicting speech gives a very general contrast to the truth of God's identity.
Taking a friend as an intimate companion does not bear on divine sonship.
The description of hypocrites has no relevant relation to the focus.
Taking a way to one's Lord shares the verb only and does not clarify the claim.
The demand for the promised judgment is unrelated to divine sonship.
Taking a way to one's Lord shares the verb only and does not clarify the claim.
Rejects seeking honor through false protectors, a distant parallel to misplacing divine prerogative.
Affirms the one God as al-Rahman, supplying a monotheistic frame against the filial attribution.
Treating signs as mockery is a generic form of religious rejection.
Unequivocally denies both begetting and being begotten.
Condemns false speech in general, without a specific connection to divine sonship.
Explicitly declares that God has not taken a child, alongside His lack of partner or need for helper.
The human misreading of prosperity and hardship is unrelated.
Taking one's desire as a god is a related distortion of divine authority, though not filial attribution.
Rules on human kinship and marriage do not clarify the focus claim.
Human parent-child relations provide only distant lexical contrast.
Rejects powerless intercessory deities before al-Rahman, supporting exclusive divine authority.
Explicitly denies that the sovereign Creator has taken a child or has a partner in dominion.
Calling revelation ancient tales is a general false labeling of divine communication.
Rejects the premise of God taking a son and affirms His oneness and irresistible power.
Calls for repentance and names God forgiving and merciful, without stating the underlying false claim.
Uses ordinary human adoption as the relevant contrast to the impossible divine attribution.
Satan's claim to take a portion of God's servants is unrelated to divine sonship.
Rejects taking any protector besides the self-sufficient Creator, a related affirmation of exclusive dependence.
The heavens nearly rupturing evokes the grave cosmic offense developed explicitly around the focus, though this verse is general.
Human adoption of Joseph is only a lexical and conceptual contrast to the claim about God.
Attributes seamless creation to al-Rahman, supporting His creative sovereignty rather than a need for offspring.
Introduces a resurrection-denying statement, not the false filial attribution.
Commands taking the one Lord as trustee, a distant contrast to assigning other relationships to God.
Condemns taking the calf as an object of worship, a related rejection of false divine assignment.
The command to seek forgiveness does not clarify the focus claim.
Solomon's prayer for mercy and mention of his parents is not materially related.
The messenger as mercy to the worlds gives broad context for mercy but not sonship.
Moses' plea for forgiveness and mercy after the earthquake is unrelated.
A skeptical statement about resurrection is only a generic parallel to false doctrine.
The believers' pledge includes family-related prohibitions but does not address divine sonship.
A prayer for mercy gives only broad thematic contact through the divine attribute.
Sole worship and kindness to parents are too general to clarify the filial attribution.
The accusation that Salih is bewitched is unrelated.
The affirmation that God is Lord and the call to steadfastness provide only general monotheistic context.
The rise of Thamud's most wretched man is unrelated.
God's mercy and punishment provide broad theological context but no sonship connection.
Human emergence from the earth does not clarify the claim.
God's self-sufficiency and mercy support the denial that He needs descendants or depends on a lineage.
Noah's plea for help against deniers is unrelated.
The call to fear God for mercy does not bear on divine sonship.
The account of sorcery and its harm does not clarify the attribution of a son.
Appeals to al-Rahman for help against people's descriptions, a broad but relevant repudiation of false descriptions of God.
God's origination of heaven and earth by decree supplies the same creation-based answer to the claim that He needs a child.
Places Jesus' creation alongside Adam's, directly countering any inference from Jesus' birth to divine sonship.
Rules out a divinely taught human prophet directing people to take him as lord besides God.
Denies that a prophet could command the worship of angels or prophets, reinforcing the rejection of creature-deification.
Calls Jesus the messenger and word of God, forbids saying "Three," and declares that God is too exalted to have a son.
States that neither the Messiah nor the angels disdain being servants of God, reinforcing the servant status opposed to sonship.
Rejects identifying the Messiah son of Mary with God and affirms God's power over the Messiah, his mother, and all creation.
Condemns saying that God is the Messiah son of Mary and records Jesus' call to worship God alone.
Rejects the claim that God is one of three and reasserts that there is only one God.
Describes the Messiah and his mother as human servants who both ate food, countering their elevation beyond creaturehood.
Explicitly condemns attributing sons and daughters to God without knowledge while associating partners with Him.
Asks how the Originator of heaven and earth could have a child without a consort and affirms that He created everything.
Directly reports and condemns the claims that Ezra or the Messiah is God's son.
Condemns taking religious authorities and the Messiah as lords besides the one God, the wider error behind false filial elevation.
Condemns assigning daughters to God while claiming for themselves what they prefer, a parallel false attribution of offspring.
Exposes those who attribute to God what they themselves dislike, including the wider polemic against false offspring claims.
Forbids false verbal attributions about God, directly relevant to the form of the focus assertion.
Challenges the incoherent claim that God chose sons for people while taking female angels for Himself, calling it a grave saying.
Says the claim that God has taken a son rests on no knowledge and is an enormity uttered from their mouths.
Jesus identifies himself as a servant of God who received scripture and prophethood, directly opposing divine sonship.
Jesus declares that God is his Lord and the people's Lord and commands worship of Him alone.
Notes the factions' disagreement about Jesus, framing the dispute resolved by the surrounding denial of sonship.
Immediate continuation: the claim that al-Rahman has a son is characterized as a monstrous assertion.
Immediate continuation: the heavens, earth, and mountains are depicted as nearly collapsing because of this assertion.
States that every being in the heavens and earth comes to al-Rahman only as a servant.
Affirms that al-Rahman has fully enumerated and counted all creatures, excluding any independent filial status.
States that every creature will come to God alone on the Day of Resurrection, completing the servanthood rebuttal.
Challenges the claimants' allocation of daughters to their Lord and sons to themselves.
Questions whether angels were created female while the claimants witnessed it, exposing the claim's lack of knowledge.
Explicitly identifies the statement "God has begotten" as part of the claimants' fabrication.
Directly reports the assertion that God has begotten and calls its speakers liars.
Challenges the supposed divine preference for daughters over sons, continuing the rebuttal of attributed offspring.
Condemns treating a servant from God's creation as a portion belonging to Him, a related false partitioning of divine relation.
Exposes the claim that the angels, servants of al-Rahman, are female, another unsupported offspring-like attribution.
Introduces the dispute provoked by the example of the son of Mary, relevant to the surrounding Christological polemic.
Defines Jesus as only a servant upon whom God bestowed favor, countering his elevation to divine sonship.
Challenges the claimants' distribution of males to themselves and females to God.
Calls that proposed distribution unjust, continuing the rejection of attributed offspring.
Denies authority and knowledge for the names and claims invented about alleged divine beings.
Condemns naming angels with female names, another unsupported assertion about God's servants.
Affirms God's absolute oneness, the theological premise of the ensuing denial of begetting.
Declares God self-sufficient, excluding any need for offspring or lineage.
Denies that anything is comparable to God, reinforcing the rejection of a creaturely parent-child relation.
Jesus disavows telling people to take him and his mother as gods, directly rejecting the elevation of creatures that underlies sonship claims.
Jesus identifies God as his Lord and their Lord and limits his message to worship of God alone.
